ogTitle: 10 Best Attractions in Sing Buri 2026 — Temples, the Bang Rachan Legend & Riverside Cafes
ogDesc: A giant reclining Buddha, the legend of Bang Rachan camp, a retro market, the bodhi-tree chapel, Wat Amphawan and garden cafes along the Chao Phraya — 10 Sing Buri attractions that never disappoint, plus trip-planning tips.
eyebrow: Local picks from Sing Buri · Updated 2026
intro: Sing Buri is a small town on the Chao Phraya just over an hour's drive from Bangkok, yet it packs in historic temples, the legend of the Bang Rachan heroes, and pretty riverside corners that easygoing travelers fall for — from a giant reclining Buddha and a retro market to garden cafes and a Thai buffalo farm. This guide gathers 10 attractions you shouldn't miss, with zones, atmosphere, and tips for fitting everything into a single day.
chips: 🌳 Bodhi-tree chapel on the Chao Phraya

blocks.html:
Sing Buri's charm is how close everything sits together — a short drive covers every style of stop. The riverside town center has old temples and a long stretch of street art along the flood barrier, perfect for an evening stroll in the cool breeze. The Khai Bang Rachan side is the history zone, home to the Heroes Memorial Park and the retro Thai market where vendors genuinely dress in traditional chong kraben and sabai. Follow the river up through In Buri and Phrom Buri and you'll find an old chapel wrapped whole in bodhi-tree roots, a serene and shady meditation temple, and a glasshouse garden cafe you could lounge at all day. There's no need to rush here — work through the spots one at a time at your own pace.

The highlight locals consider the pride of the province is Phra Non Chaksi at Wat Phra Non Chaksi Worawihan, a reclining Buddha over 47 meters long and one of the largest in Thailand — every visit to Sing Buri should include paying respects there. Right next door, the Khao Ngam Thai Buffalo Conservation Center lets you hand-feed beautifully horned buffaloes up close. Over on the Bang Rachan side lives the legend of the 11 village leaders, told and retold for centuries, and you can't skip Wat Amphawan, the famous meditation temple in the lineage of Luang Pho Charan Thitadhammo, where people travel from across the country for vipassana retreats. Old temples, a retro market, cafes, and farmstays — together they make Sing Buri far more fun to explore than you'd expect.

blocks.name: Wat Phra Non Chaksi Worawihan
blocks.area: Chak Si Subdistrict, Mueang Sing Buri District
blocks.signature: A giant reclining Buddha just over 47 meters long — among the largest in Thailand — in Ayutthaya-era style
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Phra Non Chaksi Worawihan is a third-class royal temple of the worawihan rank in Chak Si Subdistrict, about 4 kilometers from Sing Buri town. The highlight everyone comes for is "Phra Non Chaksi," a giant reclining Buddha measuring 47 meters 42 centimeters long — one of the largest reclining Buddhas in Thailand (many sources rank it among the country's biggest). It's Ayutthaya-era art, and plenty of reviewers say the face looks gentle, serene and truly beautiful. Step inside the wihan and you have to crane your neck to take in the whole statue. A great fit for temple-goers, history lovers, and families bringing older relatives on an easy trip near Bangkok.

Beyond the reclining Buddha there's plenty more to see: the Phra Kaew and Phra Kan images, a stone Buddha finished in lacquer and gold leaf, teak pillars carved with remarkably deep and intricate patterns, and a small museum keeping antiques and old banknotes. A large Sala tree stands in front of the wihan, and the grounds are shady and peaceful. Reviewers like how well organized the temple is — there are rest pavilions, a fish-feeding spot, and on weekends and holidays a tram circles the grounds from around 9am to 3pm. Kids enjoy these little corners.

There's no entry fee — donate as you wish. The parking lot is large and shaded, and the front and edges of the temple are lined with food stalls and Sing Buri OTOP souvenir shops; pick up processed Mae La snakehead fish or local sweets to take home. The temple is open for worship every day, with the popular window around 08:00–16:00 (sometimes it opens earlier). If you want to practice meditation, the temple runs free vipassana retreats on the 4th–10th of every month.

It's popular because it's Sing Buri's signature temple — easy to reach and complete for merit-making, with both the giant reclining Buddha and old craftsmanship to admire. Reviews on travel platforms rate it well and place it among the province's top attractions. Keep in mind it's a sacred site: dress modestly, remove your shoes before entering the wihan, and weekdays are much quieter than weekends when crowds arrive and every stall is open.
mustOrder: Pay respects to Phra Non Chaksi, the 47-meter reclining Buddha
See the Phra Kaew and Phra Kan images and the carved teak pillars
Ride the tram around the grounds (weekends/holidays)
Browse the OTOP souvenir market in front of the temple
blocks.bestFor: Temple-goers and families after an easy merit-making trip near Bangkok

blocks.name: Wat Phikun Thong (Luang Pho Yai)
blocks.area: Phikun Thong Subdistrict, Tha Chang District, Sing Buri
blocks.signature: Phra Phuttha Suwan Mongkhon Maha Muni — the giant gold-mosaic 'Luang Pho Yai' Buddha in the blessing-granting posture, set on a wide plaza
blocks.descHtml:
If you're in Sing Buri looking for a temple that's big, beautiful, and full of stories, Wat Phikun Thong (a royal temple) in Phikun Thong Subdistrict, Tha Chang District, is one of the most popular picks. Locals call it "Wat Luang Pho Pae" because it was the temple of Luang Pho Pae, a revered monk respected across the country. The star here is "Luang Pho Yai," or Phra Phuttha Suwan Mongkhon Maha Muni — a giant golden Buddha in the blessing-granting posture with a lap width of 11 wa 2 sok, covered entirely in gleaming gold mosaic and standing prominently in the middle of a wide plaza. Everyone ends up craning their necks for a photo with it. Ideal for merit-makers, families bringing older relatives to pay respects, and anyone after a quiet escape near Bangkok.

Beyond Luang Pho Yai, don't miss paying respects to Luang Pho Pae's preserved body and visiting the Luang Pho Pae Museum, which displays his biography and monastic belongings. Around the grounds there's a cloister gallery housing Buddha images for each day of the week, a large Phra Sangkachai statue, and a Ganesha shrine. Kids can buy fish food and scatter it for the fish by the pond. A full loop of the temple doesn't take long but feels thoroughly rewarding.

The grounds are shady and clean, and the tree-lined approach road is green enough that many count it as a photo spot in its own right. Real reviews praise the beautiful big Buddha and the spacious, easy-to-walk plaza; only a few note the restrooms could be kept cleaner. There's also a local market in front of the temple for snacks and souvenirs before you head out. Entry is free — donate as you wish. Open daily around 08:00–16:30.

It's popular because it bundles everything temple visitors want into one place: a landmark-scale Buddha, a monk people deeply revere, and wide, walkable grounds that suit families. Dress modestly for the temple, come from morning to late morning for the best light before the crowds, and in some years during the cool season there are flower fields nearby for an extra photo stop.
mustOrder: Pay respects to Luang Pho Yai, the giant gold-mosaic Buddha
Visit Luang Pho Pae's preserved body + the Luang Pho Pae Museum
Walk the cloister of day-of-the-week Buddhas + Phra Sangkachai
Feed the fish by the pond + browse the local market out front
blocks.bestFor: Merit-makers and families — best from morning to late morning

blocks.name: Bang Rachan Camp Heroes Memorial Park (Heroes Monument)
blocks.area: Bang Rachan Subdistrict, Khai Bang Rachan District, Sing Buri
blocks.signature: Monument to the 11 Bang Rachan village leaders, a replica camp, a museum, and a shaded forest park of around 115 rai
blocks.descHtml:
If you want your Sing Buri trip to be about more than eating, the "Bang Rachan Camp Heroes Memorial Park" is a stop you shouldn't skip. It's the memorial to the villagers of Bang Rachan who banded together to fight off Burmese forces eight times in the late Ayutthaya period. The park covers around 115 rai, shaded by big trees — great for families who want kids to learn history by walking through the real thing, landmark photographers, and road-trippers who can stop here conveniently on the way to Suphan Buri.

The highlight everyone stands before is the monument to the 11 village leaders — cast figures of heroes like Nai Chan Nuat Khiao, Khun San, Nai Thaen and Phan Rueang — built by the Fine Arts Department and opened by King Rama IX in person. Next to it, a replica camp shows how the defenses looked in those days, and the history study center museum is divided into themed zones, from the heroes' biographies and camp reconstruction to Sing Buri's heritage, antique utensils, and the Mae Nam Noi kiln site. Many reviewers agree they learned more than expected, and kids enjoy wandering through.

Budget-wise it's very easy, because both the park and the museum are "free to enter." Parking is plentiful, and it's open daily 08:00–17:00 (the museum building sometimes closes earlier, around 16:30 — late morning to early afternoon is recommended). It's located in Bang Rachan Subdistrict, Khai Bang Rachan District, about 15 km from Sing Buri town along Highway 3032, an easy drive.

It's popular because it's the heart of the "Bang Rachan" story Thais know from films and school lessons. A visit combines paying respects, taking photos, and strolling the shaded park. Note that midday sun can be strong since the monument plaza is open to the sky — bring a hat or umbrella, and allow about 1–2 hours.
mustOrder: The monument to the 11 Bang Rachan village leaders
The replica camp built to historic design
The history study center museum (4 zones)
A stroll through the shaded 115-rai forest park
blocks.bestFor: Family history trips + a landmark photo stop
blocks.libCredit: Photo by Mr. Peerapong Prasutr / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

blocks.name: Ban Rachan Retro Thai Market
blocks.area: Bang Rachan Subdistrict, Khai Bang Rachan District, Sing Buri
blocks.signature: A retro market where vendors dress in chong kraben and sabai and speak old-fashioned Thai, with local dishes, traditional sweets and riverside seating — open weekends and holidays
blocks.descHtml:
If you want a market that's nothing like the usual street market, try the "Ban Rachan Retro Thai Market" inside Wat Pho Kao Ton, Bang Rachan Subdistrict, Khai Bang Rachan District, Sing Buri. The market sets up under big shade trees in the temple grounds, with vendors fully committed to traditional chong kraben and sabai dress, addressing everyone in old-fashioned polite Thai across the whole market. Walk in and it feels like stepping onto the set of a late-Ayutthaya Bang Rachan film. Great for families bringing older relatives, Thai-costume photo lovers, and anyone hunting hard-to-find local food.

The highlight is old-fashioned treats priced from ten to fifty baht. Reviewers mention thong muan crispy rolls, fresh toddy palm coconut jelly, Thai sweets served in banana leaves, and Sing Buri specialties like kun chiang sausage and krayasat. Many stalls wrap everything in banana leaves and natural packaging. There are Thai dance and Bang Rachan-style swordfighting shows in rotation, and at times a buffalo tethered in front of the market for kids to photograph. Want to get deeper into it? Thai costume rentals start around 50–100 baht, and you can wander taking photos all day.

Entry is free — no admission fee — and a budget in the low hundreds per person fills you up comfortably. The parking area is huge, fitting several hundred cars. The market has over 160 stalls and opens only on "weekends and public holidays adjoining a weekend," roughly 09:00–16:30 (come on a weekday and it's quiet with no stalls). It's about 30 km from Sing Buri town, an easy drive.

People love it because it goes all-in on the retro atmosphere for real, not just a sign at the gate — the dress, the speech, and the local food all set the mood together, and you can pay respects inside Wat Pho Kao Ton right after. Just come on the right day, avoid the harsh midday sun since it's an open-air walk, and bring cash because many stalls are run by local villagers. Arrive mid-morning for the full spread before the biggest crowds.
mustOrder: Thong muan and old-style Thai sweets in banana leaves
Fresh toddy palm coconut jelly
Kun chiang sausage and krayasat — Sing Buri souvenirs
Rent a Thai costume for photos (from ฿50–100)
blocks.bestFor: Family outings and Thai-costume photos on weekend trips
blocks.zone: Khai Bang Rachan (Wat Pho Kao Ton)
blocks.hours: 09:00–16:30, weekends and public holidays adjoining a weekend only

blocks.name: The Bodhi Tree Chapel at Wat Sai
blocks.area: Chi Nam Rai Subdistrict, In Buri District, Sing Buri
blocks.signature: A century-old chapel with bodhi-tree roots embracing its entire walls, right on the Chao Phraya River — a photo spot many haven't discovered yet
blocks.descHtml:
If you love under-the-radar spots that make you go wow the moment you see them, Wat Sai in Chi Nam Rai Subdistrict, In Buri District, is a stop you shouldn't skip in Sing Buri. The temple — originally called "Wat Thayan" — dates back to the Ayutthaya period and sits right on the Chao Phraya River. What draws crowds of photographers is the old chapel that survives as bare brick walls with no roof, wrapped entirely in the massive roots of bodhi and banyan trees, as if nature itself were propping the chapel up to keep it from collapsing. That image of roots winding around the walls under a full canopy of leaves has become the signature of the place.

Don't miss walking around the chapel walls to see how the bodhi roots grip the brick so tightly they've fused into one, going in to pay respects to Luang Pho Wat Sai (formerly called Luang Pho Khao / Luang Pho Thayan), the revered old principal Buddha inside, then stepping out to the open Chao Phraya riverbank. Late afternoon, when the light softens, is the most beautiful time to shoot — sunbeams filtering through the leaves onto the old walls give it a mystical mood. Many reviewers agree the place feels peaceful and shady, ideal for people who like old temples and unusual photo angles. It isn't a grand temple, but it has a charm all its own.

The upsides: no entry fee, parking available, and an easy wander that takes only minutes to cover — a convenient stop along an In Buri route. It's open all day (travel sources list roughly 08:00–16:00 as the best-lit, safest window). The review score sits at a solid 4.5 or so, and most visitors leave positive feedback about how undiscovered and peaceful it feels.

A few things to know: this is a semi-abandoned historic site with very old structures, so walk carefully, don't climb the walls or roots, and dress modestly since it's still a place of worship. In the rainy season paths can be slippery and mosquitoes plentiful — pack repellent to stay comfortable. If you're coming with friends or for the photos, aim for morning or late afternoon to dodge the harsh sun — you're guaranteed to head home with beautiful shots.
mustOrder: Bodhi roots embracing the entire chapel walls
Pay respects to Luang Pho Wat Sai, the old principal Buddha
Chao Phraya riverside photo corners in the late afternoon
The roofless old chapel under the tree canopy
blocks.bestFor: Hidden-gem photographers — come late afternoon for the best light

blocks.title: 🛏️ Where to Stay in Sing Buri
blocks.text: To cover every district of Sing Buri without rushing, staying a night makes everything easier. In town and along the Chao Phraya you'll find small hotels, riverside resorts, and farmstays like Baan Khao Hom, where you wake up to rice fields. Head out early to see the reclining Buddha before the crowds, then come back for an evening stroll along the riverside street art. blocks.name: Khao Ngam Thai Buffalo Conservation Center
blocks.area: Chak Si Subdistrict, Mueang Sing Buri District, Sing Buri
blocks.signature: A Thai buffalo farm with beautifully horned buffaloes of several breeds, tame enough to feed and photograph up close — open daily
blocks.descHtml:
The Khao Ngam Thai Buffalo Conservation Center is a buffalo farm tucked right beside Wat Phra Non Chaksi in Chak Si Subdistrict, only about 4 kilometers from Sing Buri town. It's a perfect stop for families with kids, or animal lovers who want to meet real live Thai buffaloes up close. Founded in 2000 by the Rotary Club of Sing Buri together with the temple, its mission is to raise and preserve Thai buffaloes so they don't disappear, now that machines have replaced buffalo power almost everywhere — so a visit doubles as sightseeing and a glimpse of an old way of life most kids today have barely encountered.

The can't-miss highlight is feeding the buffaloes yourself. The animals here are very tame — you can walk right up and hand-feed them. Past visitors agree ripe bananas are their favorite, so bring a bunch along if you like, or buy the grass and feed the center has ready. The farm keeps several breeds, including pale albino buffaloes with strikingly light coloring and buffaloes with gracefully curved horns that live up to the name "Khao Ngam" (beautiful horns). You can take photos closer than almost anywhere else, and kids love the hands-on contact instead of just watching from a distance.

As for admission, most visits involve no fixed ticket — it runs on donations and buffalo-feed contributions, so you'll spend very little. It's open daily around 08:00–18:00; the sun from late morning through afternoon can be hot, so morning or evening is more comfortable, and the buffaloes are in a better mood then too. Another plus: it sits right next to Wat Phra Non Chaksi and its giant reclining Buddha, so a single trip covers both temple merit-making and buffalo time — which is why it's become such a popular stop for anyone driving through Sing Buri.

A few things to know: buffaloes are big animals — tame or not, follow the staff's guidance, keep noise down so you don't startle them, and keep small children close. Some ground is bare earth that can muddy your shoes, so wear a pair you don't mind getting dirty. All in all it's a simple attraction that's both fun and educational — ideal for a short stop of about an hour on a Sing Buri trip.
mustOrder: Feed the buffaloes yourself (ripe bananas are the favorite)
Up-close photos with beautifully horned and albino buffaloes
Pop next door to the reclining Buddha at Wat Phra Non Chaksi
tags: Next to Wat Phra Non Chaksi
blocks.bestFor: Families with kids and animal lovers — visit morning or evening

blocks.name: Wat Amphawan
blocks.signature: A meditation temple in the lineage of Luang Pho Charan Thitadhammo — shady and serene, with his preserved body enshrined for veneration
blocks.descHtml:
When it comes to meditation temples known across the country, "Wat Amphawan" in Phrom Buri, Sing Buri, is always near the top of the list. This is the temple of Luang Pho Charan Thitadhammo (Phra Dhammasinghaburacharn), who laid the foundation for vipassana practice in the Satipatthana 4 tradition — the rising-falling method — that became the model for meditation centers all over Thailand. The temple itself dates to the Ayutthaya period, sits on the Chao Phraya River, and is shaded by big trees, with the kind of cool, quiet atmosphere that hushes the noise in your head the moment you walk in. It suits both blessing-seekers and anyone looking for a peaceful corner to rest their mind for a day.

The highlight every visitor stops at is the Phra Chedi Dhammasinghaburachariyanusorn, standing prominently near the temple entrance. Inside rests the preserved body of Luang Pho Charan, open for followers to go up and pay respects daily from around 8am to 5pm. Many reviewers describe getting goosebumps and feeling genuinely calm and fulfilled up there. Beyond the chedi there's the old ubosot, a Lopburi-era naga-sheltered Buddha, and several more shrines and sacred spots to visit around the grounds. The stairway up the chedi is fairly wide, though reviews warn it gets slippery on rainy days — shoes with good grip help.

There's no entry fee; your only real costs are donations and travel. For serious practice, the temple runs retreat courses — both Friday–Sunday sessions and sessions on Buddhist holy days and lunar quarter days — with advance registration through amphawan.net (a form that closes in the afternoon). The schedule is intense: up at 3:30am for chanting, walking meditation, and sitting meditation, with lodging and meals provided; no makeup, and modest white clothing is required. Casual visitors who just want to pay respects don't need to register — walk in and explore freely.

The location couldn't be easier to find: the temple sits right on the Asian Highway (Highway 1) at Phrom Buri, about an hour and a half's drive from Bangkok — a stop many people heading north pull into for a quick round of merit-making. The temple scores a high 4.7 from thousands of Google reviews, a sign that visitors leave genuinely impressed and tell others. Dress modestly with shoulders and knees covered in the sacred areas, and come in the early morning or late afternoon for the most tranquil atmosphere.
mustOrder: Pay respects to Luang Pho Charan's preserved body at the Phra Chedi Dhammasinghaburachariyanusorn
Practice Satipatthana 4 vipassana meditation (the rising-falling method)
Visit the old ubosot and the Lopburi-era naga-sheltered Buddha
Stroll the shady corners along the Chao Phraya River
blocks.bestFor: Meditation and merit-making — a quiet place to rest the mind
blocks.zone: Phrom Buri (Chao Phraya riverside, on the Asian Highway)
blocks.hours: 08:00–17:00 daily (paying respects at the chedi) · temple grounds ~04:00–18:00

blocks.name: Chao Phraya Riverside Street Art (Sing Buri Old Town)
blocks.area: Along the Chao Phraya flood barrier in front of Sing Buri Municipality (Bang Rachan Bridge–100th Anniversary Memorial Bridge)
blocks.signature: Street art along roughly 3.4 km of flood-barrier wall telling Sing Buri's story, with a riverside promenade for sunset views
blocks.descHtml:
If you love riverside photo walks, this is the spot you have to hit in Sing Buri town. The street art along the Chao Phraya flood barrier is one continuous stretch of murals on the flood-protection wall, running from Bang Rachan Bridge to the 100th Anniversary Memorial Bridge — about 3.4 kilometers in total, making it the longest painted flood-barrier wall in Thailand. Work began in early 2023, with professional artists, volunteers, and local students all pitching in to add color. Great for art lovers, families out with the kids, and photographers hunting unusual frames.

The highlight is that the murals genuinely tell Sing Buri's story — riverside life, the history of the Bang Rachan heroes, brightly colored Chao Phraya fish and river creatures, and the province's signature local goods. Keep walking and new check-in corners appear the whole way. On the other side of the path is the wide Chao Phraya itself; reviewers agree evenings bring a cool breeze and beautiful sunsets, and after dark the wall lighting shifts the mood into something else entirely.

Budget is a non-issue, because it's a public riverside space in front of the town — free to walk, no entry fee, open at all hours. It runs through the heart of old Sing Buri along Wilaichit Road, Bang Phutsa Subdistrict, Mueang District; park along the road and walk from there. Late afternoon to evening gets you the best light without the heat. The spot keeps growing in fame as a new landmark the province is pushing hard, and it pairs easily with the old town, temples, and riverside restaurants in the same neighborhood.

Things to know: the walkway is a long, open-air stretch with little shade, so carry a hat and water. To capture every section, allow time to walk or cycle the full length, and watch for cars on the road that runs beside the barrier.
mustOrder: 3.4 km of murals telling Sing Buri's story (Thailand's longest)
The Chao Phraya riverside promenade at sunset
Check-in corners with Bang Rachan heroes and riverside-life murals
The illuminated walls after dark
blocks.hours: Open at all hours (public walkway) · best late afternoon–evening

blocks.name: Rai Sing Kaset (Vazana Coffee House)
blocks.area: Thong En Subdistrict, In Buri District, Sing Buri
blocks.signature: A glasshouse cafe set in a garden, with a big fish pond, waterside seating, and a menu of drinks, bakes and mains — open daily
blocks.descHtml:
Rai Sing Kaset — better known as Vazana Coffee House — is a glasshouse cafe set in a garden in Thong En Subdistrict, In Buri District, Sing Buri. It's a stop made for cafe-hoppers who like lounging in leafy surroundings, families with kids, or anyone bringing the dog along. The place is designed as agro-tourism meets cafe, with seasonal flower beds, fruit trees, and several seating zones to suit your mood — the cool air-conditioned glasshouse, out in the garden, or by the water.

The highlights people mention most are the photogenic glasshouse, photo corners scattered across the garden, the big fish pond kids love watching, and the breezy waterside seating. The menu runs wide, from drinks and house-roasted specialty coffee to homemade bakes like banoffee cake and brownies, all the way to proper mains. Many reviewers praise the americano and the fish dishes, and the desserts get good marks too — though a few note some drinks can be inconsistent, so ordering the signatures first is the safer bet.

On budget: there's no entry fee, you can wander and take photos for free, and there's free Wi-Fi and ample parking. Expect roughly 200–400 baht per person depending on whether you stop at coffee and cake or stay for a meal. The location is about 2 kilometers past Tak Fa Bridge — coming from Bangkok, turn in at the bridge and the cafe is on the right. Open daily: Monday–Friday 09:00–18:00, weekends and long holidays until 20:00.

It ranks among Sing Buri's most popular cafes because it gathers everything people love in one place — the lush green garden, the photogenic glasshouse, the fish pond and waterside corners, and plenty of space to roam — suiting families and friend groups alike. Note that weekends get busy; come in the morning for uncontested photo spots, and double-check closing times since weekdays and weekends differ.
mustOrder: Specialty coffee / the much-praised americano
Banoffee cake + homemade brownies
Fish dishes (there's a fish pond in the garden)
Glasshouse photo corners + waterside seating
blocks.bestFor: Cafe photographers, families with kids or dogs, easy waterside lounging

blocks.name: Baan Khao Hom Farmstay
blocks.signature: A full agro-tourism farmstay — feed the fish and buffaloes, cycle or ride ATVs through the rice fields, sleep in wooden houses, with a cafe and lodging on site
blocks.descHtml:
If you want to escape Bangkok and sleep in the middle of the rice fields without a long drive, "Baan Khao Hom Farmstay" in Hua Phai Subdistrict, Mueang Sing Buri District, is the place people keep talking about. It's a full-scale agro-tourism farmstay with Thai-style wooden houses set among the paddies, surrounded by an organic vegetable garden, a lotus pond, wetlands, and farm animals including albino buffaloes, ducks, chickens and geese. Ideal for families who want the kids close to nature, friend groups after a laid-back night in the fields, or working people who need a genuine night off to reset.

The highlight reviewers agree on is an activity list so packed there's hardly time to get bored — feeding the fish, tending the albino buffaloes, cycling through the paddies in the morning and evening, ATV rides (usually an extra charge), tractor rides, driving the paddle-wheel irrigation boat, climbing the birdwatching tower, and lift-net fishing. Early risers can offer alms to monks in front of the house, and you get to see real rice farming up close, from planting through the mill to vacuum-packing. The must-try is the countryside dinner set: shrimp-paste chili dip served with fresh vegetables, sun-dried snakehead fish, fried mackerel, spicy tom saep soup, and tri-color organic rice (jasmine, brown, and riceberry). Breakfast is pork rice porridge with old-style khanom krok.

Value-wise it holds up well: most reviews cite packages of around 750–850 baht per person covering one night's stay, two meals, snacks, and nearly all activities (except the ATV, which costs extra). Rooms are a handful of Thai-style wooden houses in 2-, 3-, and 4-bed layouts with en-suite bathrooms and air-conditioning. It's a little over 20 km from Sing Buri town, about a 2-hour drive from Bangkok. The Google rating sits around 4.3 stars, with frequent praise for the kind owners who look after guests like family and the evening paddy views that photograph beautifully from every angle.

Things to know: the farmstay works mainly on advance booking and usually opens Friday–Sunday (registered hours are 09:00–18:00). Call ahead to check schedules and book your stay via the Baan Khao Hom Sing Buri Facebook page or 082-724-0322, since rooms are limited and long weekends fill up fast. Pack mosquito repellent and a light jacket too — out in the open fields the breeze turns cool and mosquitoes come with the territory.

blocks.title: Know Before You Go: Sing Buri

items.title: Rent a car or have Grab ready
items.text: The attractions are spread across several districts and public transport within the province is limited, so your own car or a rental is by far the easiest. Grab works in town but can be hard to find around Bang Rachan and In Buri — plan your transport in advance.

items.title: Carry cash
items.text: The retro Thai market, roadside food stalls, and buffalo-feed donations at the farm mostly take cash, and many small vendors have no card machines. Small notes and coins keep things moving smoothly.

items.title: Temples in the morning, riverside in the evening
items.text: Sing Buri's midday sun is fierce. Visit the temples and the memorial park in the morning while it's cooler, then save the open-air photo spots like the bodhi-tree chapel and the riverside street art for the evening breeze and golden light.

items.title: Check the retro market's opening days
items.text: The Ban Rachan Retro Thai Market at Wat Pho Kao Ton opens only on weekends and holidays. If you want the full scene of vendors in traditional dress and the local food, time your trip for a weekend.

items.title: Dress modestly at temples
items.text: Wat Phra Non Chaksi, Wat Phikun Thong, and Wat Amphawan are sacred places. Dress modestly with shoulders and knees covered, remove your shoes before entering the halls, and keep quiet — especially at Wat Amphawan, where people come to meditate.

items.title: English menus are rare
items.text: Sing Buri is a local town with few English signs or menus. A translation app helps when ordering food; locals are kind and eager to help, and a smile plus pointing at pictures gets you a long way.

blocks.title: Planning Sing Buri in One Day
blocks.html:
Routing by zone makes the day flow best. Start the morning in the Chak Si area of town: pay respects to the reclining Buddha at Wat Phra Non Chaksi Worawihan before the sun gets strong, then continue to the Khao Ngam Thai Buffalo Conservation Center in the same subdistrict for a happy round of buffalo feeding and photos. Next, drive over to the Khai Bang Rachan side for the Heroes Memorial Park, and if it's a weekend or holiday, have lunch at the Ban Rachan Retro Thai Market inside Wat Pho Kao Ton — a ฿100–200 budget fills you up comfortably.

In the afternoon, work your way north to In Buri: photograph the bodhi-tree chapel at Wat Sai on the Chao Phraya, then rest with a coffee at Rai Sing Kaset (Vazana Coffee House), the glasshouse cafe in a garden. Close the evening with a stroll along the street art on the Chao Phraya barrier in the old town, catching the cool breeze and the sunset. If you have more than a day, add the meditation temple Wat Amphawan and an overnight stay at Baan Khao Hom Farmstay.

blocks.text: Fitting every Sing Buri spot into one day can be a stretch. Stay a night and travel without rushing — browse hotels in town and along the Chao Phraya, compare prices, and book in a few clicks.

faq.q: First time in Sing Buri — what can't I miss?
faq.a: The spot locals consider the pride of the province is Phra Non Chaksi at Wat Phra Non Chaksi Worawihan, a giant reclining Buddha over 47 meters long and one of the largest in Thailand — every visit should include paying respects there. History lovers shouldn't miss the Bang Rachan Camp Heroes Memorial Park and the legend of the 11 village leaders.

faq.q: What kinds of highlights does Sing Buri offer?
faq.a: A bit of everything in one town. For temples and sacred sites there are Wat Phra Non Chaksi, Wat Phikun Thong (Luang Pho Yai), and Wat Amphawan in the Luang Pho Charan meditation lineage. For history there's Bang Rachan camp and the Ban Rachan Retro Thai Market. For riverside photos there's the bodhi-tree chapel at Wat Sai and the street art along the Chao Phraya barrier. And for laid-back stops there's the garden cafe Rai Sing Kaset and the Khao Ngam Thai buffalo farm.

faq.q: Do Sing Buri attractions charge entry fees?
faq.a: Mostly free. All the temples, the Bang Rachan Heroes Memorial Park, the bodhi-tree chapel at Wat Sai, and the riverside street art have no entry fee. The Khao Ngam Thai Buffalo Conservation Center is free to visit with buffalo feed by donation. The retro Thai market is free to enter — you only pay for food, around ฿100–200. The Rai Sing Kaset cafe has free entry with a budget of ฿200–400 per person, while Baan Khao Hom Farmstay is an overnight package at roughly ฿750–850 per person.

faq.q: How do I get to Sing Buri, and is parking easy?
faq.a: It's about an hour and a half to two hours' drive from Bangkok along the Asian Highway. Wat Amphawan sits right on the highway at Phrom Buri and is very easy to reach. Nearly every attraction is a temple or park with a large free parking lot. A private car is the most convenient option, since the sights are spread across several districts and public transport within the province is limited.

faq.q: What are the opening hours of Sing Buri's attractions?
faq.a: The temples and the Khao Ngam buffalo conservation center open roughly 08:00–18:00 daily, and the Rai Sing Kaset cafe opens every day. The Ban Rachan Retro Thai Market opens only on weekends and holidays. Open-air photo spots like the bodhi-tree chapel and the riverside street art can be visited all day. To dodge the midday sun, do the temples in the morning and save the riverside corners for the evening.
